Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Now I have the actual text of Prop 43. It's ACA 22 (2025-2026 Regular Session, Resolution Chapter 132, Statutes of 2026). It adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A:

(a) Beginning Jan 1, 2027, no local government, including the electorate exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless approved by two-thirds vote (with existing exceptions in Section 4 of XIII A — that's the existing two-thirds for special taxes; and XIII C(2)(d) — property-related fees? and XIII D(3)(a)(2)?).

(b) No local government, including the electorate, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in XIII D(3)(a)(1) (which is the exception for bonded indebtedness). So this also blocks new "mansion tax"-style... wait, no. Ad valorem property taxes based on value. Actually Measure ULA is a real estate transfer tax (documentary transfer tax), not an ad valorem tax. Prop 43(b) prohibits new ad valorem property taxes (taxes based on property value) except for bonded indebtedness voter-approved under XIII D. This prevents localities from creating new value-based property taxes via initiative — like the "split roll"-style local taxes or SF's proposed "parcel tax based on square footage"? 1. Two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including citizen-initiated ones (impose, extend, or increase).
2. Ban on new local ad valorem (value-based) property taxes, including via initiative, except for bond repayment under XIII D.

The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group who brought California the landmark Proposition 13, is now sponsoring Proposition 43 — a measure to make it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes.

Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)

This November, California voters will consider Proposition 43 — a measure aimed at making it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes. # Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
...
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

content.thinking:
Now I have the actual text of Prop 43. It's ACA 22 (2025-2026 Regular Session, Resolution Chapter 132, Statutes of 2026). It adds Section 4.5 to Article XIII A:

(a) Beginning Jan 1, 2027, no local government, including the electorate exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless approved by two-thirds vote (with existing exceptions in Section 4 of XIII A — that's the existing two-thirds for special taxes; and XIII C(2)(d) — property-related fees? and XIII D(3)(a)(2)?).

(b) No local government, including the electorate, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in XIII D(3)(a)(1) (which is the exception for bonded indebtedness). So this also blocks new "mansion tax"-style... wait, no. Ad valorem property taxes based on value. Actually Measure ULA is a real estate transfer tax (documentary transfer tax), not an ad valorem tax. Prop 43(b) prohibits new ad valorem property taxes (taxes based on property value) except for bonded indebtedness voter-approved under XIII D. This prevents localities from creating new value-based property taxes via initiative — like the "split roll"-style local taxes or SF's proposed "parcel tax based on square footage"? Square footage isn't ad valorem. Hmm. This (b) provision blocks initiatives that would impose property-value-based taxes, which some cities have considered (e.g., a tax on property value to fund services). SF's 2018 Prop C was a gross receipts tax. LA's ULA is a transfer tax.

Note the SacBee article said: "Prop. 43 would also generally prohibit local governments from creating new taxes based on property values, with exceptions for certain voter-approved taxes used to repay bonds."

So Prop 43 has two components:
1. Two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including citizen-initiated ones (impose, extend, or increase).
2. Ban on new local ad valorem (value-based) property taxes, including via initiative, except for bond repayment under XIII D.

This was placed on the ballot by the Legislature via ACA 22 (2025-26). The rebuttal says "The Legislature's nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot" — let me verify that claim. ACA 22 in 2025-2026 session... I recall in 2025, Assemblymember... hmm. Let me search for ACA 22 California 2025 Aguiar-Curry? Actually I don't remember. Let me search for the vote count.

The deal background: In June 2024, the Legislature passed ACA 13 (which would have required any initiative that raises vote thresholds to pass by that same threshold — aimed at defeating the Taxpayer Protection Act). Then a deal was struck: the Newsom administration, legislative leaders, and HJTA/business agreed to (1) remove ACA 13 from the 2024 ballot, (2) HJTA withdraws... wait, actually the TPA proponents refused to withdraw? No — the sequence was: The California Supreme Court removed the TPA (Initiative 21-0042A1) from the ballot on June 20, 2024. But before that, in June 2024, there was a deal: the Legislature would remove ACA 13 in exchange for the business community withdrawing the TPA. The court ruling made that moot. Then as part of the deal, the Legislature agreed to place this compromise measure (two-thirds for citizen special taxes) on the 2026 ballot — that became ACA 22? Hmm, wait. Actually I recall the deal in June 2024 included placing a compromise on the 2026 ballot. Let me verify by searching.

Actually, I recall: "As part of the deal to get the California Business Roundtable and HJTA to withdraw their initiative (the Taxpayer Protection Act), the Legislature agreed to place ACA 22 on the 2026 ballot." But the Supreme Court removed the TPA before signatures were withdrawn... The TPA had already qualified. The court removed it June 20, 2024. Then... hmm, so why did the compromise still go forward? I believe the deal was struck anyway — the compromise measure was part of AB 440 (the budget trailer?) Hmm.

Let me just search for "ACA 22" California 2025 to find the legislative vehicle and vote.

Also, I want to check:
- Polling on Prop 43 (any public polls? PPIC? IGS?).
- The SF Chronicle editorial's actual recommendation (the headline "Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California's tax system" — need to see if they recommend yes or no).
- The Mercury News endorsement (yes) and Sacramento Bee (no).
- KQED pieces for balance.

Then I'll decide. Let me also consider the broader context: Prop 40 (billionaire tax) on the same ballot; Prop 42 (property taxes) — Prop 42 appears to be the "Taxpayer Protection Act"-style initiative? Wait, the text PDF shows "TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 42 CONTINUED" right before Prop 43, and Prop 42's text includes a provision about "continuous appropriation... to defend this act" — that's the California Business Roundtable's "Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act" reborn? CalMatters lists Prop 42 as "Property taxes". Interesting: Prop 42 might be a competing measure — the more restrictive tax proposal that the deal was designed to keep off the ballot — apparently it got on the 2026 ballot anyway via initiative! Let me check. If both 42 and 43 pass, there may be a conflict provision. Hmm, but the user only asks about Prop 43.

Actually wait — the CalMatters listing: Prop 40 Billionaire tax, Prop 41 Tax audits, Prop 42 Property taxes. And there was a CalMatters article "The billionaire tax could be defeated by two other tax measures" (Props 41/42). And the text PDF includes Prop 42's text with the "defend this act" provision — that language is typical of the Business Roundtable measures. So Prop 42 might be the new HJTA/Business Roundtable initiative — the "Taxpayer Protection Act 2.0"? Hmm, but the deal was supposed to keep that off the ballot. Interesting, but tangential.

Let me focus: I need to decide a recommendation on Prop 43. Let me gather a few more pieces:

1. ACA 22 legislative vote (to evaluate "nearly unanimous" claim).
2. Polling.
3. SF Chronicle recommendation.
4. Maybe the KQED analysis.

Let me search.

1. ACA 22 - California Legislative Information - CA.gov
https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22
# ACA-22 Local taxes: limitation. (2025-2026)
...
## Bill Start
Assembly Constitutional Amendment
No. 22**
CHAPTER 132
A resolution to propose to the people of the State of California an amendment to the Constitution of the State, by adding Section 4.5 to Article XIII A thereof, relating to taxation.
...
## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST

***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

**What Prop 43 does (from the actual text, ACA 22, Wicks):**
1. Section (a): Beginning Jan 1, 2027, ALL local special taxes — including those proposed via citizen initiative — require two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase. This closes the Upland decision gap.
2. Section (b): Prohibits local governments (including via initiative) from imposing NEW ad valorem taxes on real property, except for bonded indebtedness (Art. XIII D, Sec. 3(a)(1)). This is prospective and prevents new value-based property taxes.
3. Prospective only — does not retroactively invalidate existing taxes (unlike the withdrawn HJTA initiative, which would have voided post-2022 taxes that didn't get 2/3, including LA's Measure ULA mansion tax).

**History:**
- Prop 13 (1978): two-thirds for local special taxes (as interpreted), Prop 218 (1996) reinforced.
- California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (2017): CA Supreme Court held constitutional provisions constraining "local government" don't apply to citizen initiatives; implied special taxes via initiative might need only majority.
- Subsequent cases (SF Prop C 2018 homelessness tax upheld with ~61%; Fresno Measure P parks tax upheld at 52% after litigation; Oakland; etc.) established majority-vote path for citizen-initiated special taxes.
- HJTA's Taxpayer Protection & Government Accountability Act (2024): removed from ballot by CA Supreme Court as unconstitutional revision (June 2024).
- HJTA then qualified a new initiative for 2026 (Initiative 1983 / 25-0006A1, "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13") — broader: would cap real estate transfer taxes, retroactively void taxes not passed by 2/3, etc.
- June 2026 deal: Newsom, legislative leaders, HJTA — HJTA withdraws its initiative; Legislature places ACA 22 (Wicks) on ballot instead. Passed Senate 35-1, Assembly 68-2 — nearly unanimous bipartisan support as a compromise.
- Notably, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland), the author, said she wrote it "not because I wanted it to become law. But because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out." She urged people NOT to vote for it. That's a remarkable fact: the author of the measure opposes its passage. The compromise's purpose was achieved at the ballot-deadline stage (the worse measure was withdrawn); Prop 43 passing isn't necessary to get the deal's benefit. That said, if Prop 43 fails, HJTA could come back with a new initiative in 2028 — the deal's durability might depend on Prop 43 passing? Hmm, unclear. The deal was: withdraw initiative in exchange for placing ACA 22 on ballot. If ACA 22 fails at the ballot, HJTA is free to try again in 2028. That's a strategic consideration for a voter: voting no might invite a worse measure later; voting yes entrenches the compromise.

**Endorsements:**
- Yes: HJTA, CalTax, Reform California, CA Hispanic Chambers, Family Business Assoc.; SoCal News Group (OC Register etc.), San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News editorial boards.
- No: California Democratic Party, SEIU, firefighters, teachers, school employees, housing advocates, Sierra Business Council, Californians Against Waste; Sacramento Bee, Santa Cruz Sentinel. SF Chronicle headline "Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California's tax system" — need to check the actual recommendation. Let me quickly check that. The title suggests ambivalence. Given the pattern (the Chron editorial board is moderate-liberal), and the headline "Prop 43 is absurd," they probably recommend... hmm, "but so is California's entire system of taxation" — maybe they recommend a reluctant no, or they recommend yes as a way to force tax reform? Let me fetch it. Actually — it may be paywalled. Let me try.

**Polling:**
- UC Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25): No 46%, Yes 36%, 18% undecided.
- PPIC (Oct): No 55%, Yes 42% (among likely voters, different wording).
- So Prop 43 is trailing and likely to fail. But that doesn't determine my recommendation.

**Merits analysis:**

For YES:
- Equalizes the rules: same two-thirds bar regardless of who puts a special tax on the ballot. Removes the incentive for government officials to launder taxes through allied "citizen" campaigns (e.g., Fresno, SF examples where officials were deeply involved).
- Restores the pre-2017 status quo that voters approved (Prop 13/218) and that was widely understood to apply.
- Higher bar = broader consensus for taxes that bind everyone; protects against narrow special interests passing earmarked taxes in low-turnout elections.
- Prospective only; modest; a genuine compromise that avoids far worse (retroactive invalidation of ULA etc.).
- Nearly unanimous legislative vote.

For NO:
- Supermajority requirements are anti-majoritarian: 33.4% can block 66.6%. "Minority rule."
- Makes it extremely hard to fund local services — fire, 911, roads, schools, housing, transit. Two-thirds is rarely achieved (only ~half of two-thirds measures pass; many get 55-65% and fail). E.g., Bay Area transit tax polling 54-58% would be dead under Prop 43.
- The "loophole" framing is contestable: Upland rested on a plausible reading of the constitution (initiative power is a reserved power of the people, not the government); and the people ARE the ones voting — a majority voting to tax themselves is democratic self-governance.
- Doesn't cut any existing taxes; purely makes future revenue-raising harder.
- The author herself (Wicks) doesn't want it to become law; it was leverage, not policy conviction. Many Dems voted for it as a deal, then the CA Dem Party endorsed No.

- The "loophole" framing is contestable: Upland rested on a plausible reading of the constitution (initiative power is a reserved power of the people, not the government); and the people ARE the ones voting — a majority voting to tax themselves is democratic self-governance.

The strongest argument for NO: supermajority requirements entrench minority veto and have demonstrably blocked broadly popular measures (e.g., San Diego Measure C got 65.2% and failed pre-Upland; numerous transportation measures in the 60s failed). Majority rule is the default of democracy; the initiative power belongs to the people, and a majority of voters deciding to tax themselves for services is legitimate self-determination. Also this measure piles onto Prop 13's already-strict limits.

1. Symmetry argument for YES is real but double-edged: one could also fix asymmetry by lowering government-proposed special taxes to majority (as Prop 5-style proposals attempt). Prop 43 chooses the restrictive direction.

The two-thirds requirement has produced well-documented fiscal pathologies in California (reliance on fees, debt, state bailouts; infrastructure underfunding). Extending minority veto to citizen initiatives restricts the one remaining avenue communities have. Also the "low-turnout election" argument cuts both ways — measures on general election ballots with majority votes are quite democratic.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

I've completed extensive research on this measure. Here's what I found:

**What Prop 43 does:** It amends the state constitution so that local special taxes proposed via citizen initiative (new, increased, or extended) would need two-thirds voter approval instead of a simple majority, starting Jan. 1, 2027. It also permanently bans new local property-value-based taxes. It doesn't cut any existing taxes.

**Key context:**
- This exists because of a 2017 court ruling (the *Upland* decision) that let citizen-initiated special taxes pass with a simple majority. Since then, ~two dozen measures (e.g., LA's Measure ULA "mansion tax," SF's Prop C homelessness tax) passed with between 50–66.6%.
- It was placed on the ballot nearly unanimously by the Legislature (35–1 Senate, 68–2 Assembly) purely as a compromise: the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association agreed to withdraw a far harsher, retroactive initiative in exchange. Notably, the measure's own author, Asm. Buffy Wicks, says she wrote it as leverage and doesn't want it to become law.
- Supporters: HJTA, business/taxpayer groups, OC Register, SD Union-Tribune, Mercury News. Opponents: CA Democratic Party, firefighters, teachers, nurses, SEIU, Sacramento Bee, Santa Cruz Sentinel. SF Chronicle took no position. Polls show it trailing (roughly 36–42% yes).

**My judgment:** While there's a real "level playing field" argument for closing the loophole, supermajority requirements let a one-third minority veto majority-supported funding for local services, and California's experience shows many popular measures (55–65% support) die under a two-thirds bar. The measure entrenches minority veto, restricts local self-governance further, and its own author disavows it.

**No**

Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
Proposal
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
Fiscal Effects
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments' tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.

Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services.
Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval.
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
